Shepard's high school alma mater in Derry, Pinkerton Academy, has a building named after him, and the school team is called the Astros after his career as an astronaut.[[149]](#cite_note-shepard-149) Alan B. Shepard Middle School, which opened in 1961 in [Deerfield, Illinois](/wiki/Deerfield,_Illinois "Deerfield, Illinois"), was the first building named in his honor.[[150]](#cite_note-150) [Alan B. Shepard High School](/wiki/Alan_B._Shepard_High_School "Alan B. Shepard High School"), in [Palos Heights, Illinois](/wiki/Palos_Heights,_Illinois "Palos Heights, Illinois"), which opened in 1976, was named in his honor. Framed newspapers throughout the school depict various accomplishments and milestones in Shepard's life. Additionally, an autographed plaque commemorates the dedication of the building. The school newspaper is named *Freedom 7* and the yearbook is entitled *Odyssey*.[[151]](#cite_note-151) [Blue Origin](/wiki/Blue_Origin "Blue Origin")'s suborbital space tourism rocket, the [New Shepard](/wiki/New_Shepard "New Shepard"), is named after Shepard.[[152]](#cite_note-152)

In a 2010 [Space Foundation](/wiki/Space_Foundation "Space Foundation") survey, Shepard was ranked as the ninth most popular space hero (tied with astronauts [Buzz Aldrin](/wiki/Buzz_Aldrin "Buzz Aldrin") and Gus Grissom).[[153]](#cite_note-153) In 2011, NASA honored Shepard with an Ambassador of Exploration Award, consisting of a [Moon rock](/wiki/Moon_rock "Moon rock") encased in [Lucite](/wiki/Poly(methyl_methacrylate) "Poly(methyl methacrylate)"), for his contributions to the U.S. space program. His family members accepted the award on his behalf during a ceremony on April 28 at the [United States Naval Academy Museum](/wiki/United_States_Naval_Academy_Museum "United States Naval Academy Museum") in [Annapolis, Maryland](/wiki/Annapolis,_Maryland "Annapolis, Maryland"), where it is on permanent display.[[154]](#cite_note-154) On May 4, 2011, the [U.S. Postal Service](/wiki/United_States_Postal_Service "United States Postal Service") issued a first-class stamp in Shepard's honor, the first U.S. stamp to depict a specific astron

fanoutqa_003334.t: Jim Kenney :: Mayor of Philadelphia :: Second term (2020–2024) :: COVID-19 pandemic :: chunk_0008
fanoutqa_003334.x:
Jim Kenney :: Mayor of Philadelphia :: Second term (2020–2024) :: COVID-19 pandemic :: chunk_0008
In March 2020, Kenney declared [state of emergency](/wiki/State_of_emergency "State of emergency") amid the spread of [COVID-19 pandemic](/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), caused by SARS-CoV-2. The pandemic has resulted in severe social and economic disruption around the world, including the largest global recession since the Great Depression in the 1930s. In Philadelphia, COVID has led to widespread supply shortages exacerbated by [panic buying](/wiki/Panic_buying "Panic buying"), agricultural disruption, and [food shortages](/wiki/Food_security "Food security"), as well as increased [gun violence](/wiki/Gun_violence "Gun violence"), opioid usage, and [housing insecurity](/wiki/Housing_insecurity "Housing insecurity"). Kenny has referred to COVID as a "[nuclear bomb](/wiki/Nuclear_bomb "Nuclear bomb")" because of the way it affected the city.[[41]](#cite_note-41)

See also: [Killing of Walter Wallace](/wiki/Killing_of_Walter_Wallace "Killing of Walter Wallace")

During the summer of 2020, Kenney approved the use of [CS gas](/wiki/CS_gas "CS gas") on protestors during a peaceful protest, who were blocking traffic, on [Interstate 676](/wiki/Interstate_676 "Interstate 676").[[42]](#cite_note-42)

In response to protests over the [murder of George Floyd](/wiki/Murder_of_George_Floyd "Murder of George Floyd"), Kenney had the Center City [statue](/wiki/Statue_of_Frank_Rizzo "Statue of Frank Rizzo") of [Frank Rizzo](/wiki/Frank_Rizzo "Frank Rizzo") removed in June 2020.[[43]](#cite_note-43)

Kenney was known for his outspoken feuds and reports on public figures or groups who attack his legislative agenda, image, or the city of Philadelphia. Early in his career, Kenney was known as a candid and opinionated councilman and mayor, particularly on social media platforms like [Twitter](/wiki/Twitter "Twitter").[[44]](#cite_note-44) Since his election as Mayor of Philadelphia, Kenney has taken a much more measured tone with respect to his political opponents.[[45]](#cite_note-45)

fanoutqa_012294.x:
Ryan Fitzpatrick :: Professional career :: Tampa Bay Buccaneers :: 2017 season :: chunk_0015
On May 19, 2017, the [Tampa Bay Buccaneers](/wiki/Tampa_Bay_Buccaneers "Tampa Bay Buccaneers") signed Fitzpatrick to a one-year, $3 million contract.[[107]](#cite_note-107)[[108]](#cite_note-108)[[109]](#cite_note-109)[[110]](#cite_note-110)

During a Week 6 38–33 road loss to the [Arizona Cardinals](/wiki/2017_Arizona_Cardinals_season "2017 Arizona Cardinals season"), Fitzpatrick entered the game after starter [Jameis Winston](/wiki/Jameis_Winston "Jameis Winston") suffered a shoulder injury in the second quarter. Fitzpatrick finished the game by completing 22 of 32 passes for 290 yards, three touchdowns, and two interceptions.[[111]](#cite_note-111) Three weeks later against the [New Orleans Saints](/wiki/2017_New_Orleans_Saints_season "2017 New Orleans Saints season"), Fitzpatrick entered the game after Winston suffered another shoulder injury, completing eight of 15 passes for 68 yards and a touchdown in the 30–10 road loss.[[112]](#cite_note-112) On November 6, head coach [Dirk Koetter](/wiki/Dirk_Koetter "Dirk Koetter") said that Winston would miss at least two weeks to rest his shoulder.[[113]](#cite_note-Laine-113) Fitzpatrick started in Week 10 against his former team, the [New York Jets](/wiki/2017_New_York_Jets_season "2017 New York Jets season"), throwing for 187 yards, a touchdown, and an interception as the Buccaneers won by a score of 15–10.[[114]](#cite_note-114) In the next game against the [Miami Dolphins](/wiki/2017_Miami_Dolphins_season "2017 Miami Dolphins season"), Fitzpatrick threw for 275 yards and two touchdowns as the Buccaneers won on the road by a score of 30–20.[[115]](#cite_note-115) The following week against the [Atlanta Falcons](/wiki/2017_Atlanta_Falcons_season "2017 Atlanta Falcons season"), he threw for 283 yards as the Buccaneers lost on the road by a score of 34–20.[[116]](#cite_note-116)

Fitzpatrick finished the 2017 season with 1,103 passing yards, seven touchdowns, and three interceptions to go along with 15 carries for 78 yards in six games and three starts.[[117]](#cite_note-117)

Everyone at the firm struggles to adjust to Jessica's absence. Donna takes a position as [COO](/wiki/Chief_operating_officer "Chief operating officer"), and Harvey's friend Alex Williams joins the team. Harvey begins dating Paula; Louis' sessions with his own German therapist, Stan Lipschitz, have mixed results. Rachel begins her career as an attorney, having passed the bar. Mike continues to work pro bono cases at the clinic, with Harvey's blessing, but one of the cases puts Alex, Harvey, and others at risk. Louis and Sheila Sasz, Head of Admissions for Columbia University, reconnect, as does [Jessica with her family in Chicago](/wiki/Pearson_(TV_series) "Pearson (TV series)"). Mike and Rachel accept an offer to found and run their own [public interest law](/wiki/Public_interest_law "Public interest law") firm in [Seattle](/wiki/Seattle "Seattle") that takes on [class-action suits](/wiki/Class_action "Class action"), and get married before leaving. As the season closes, a case that puts Specter Litt in danger is the work of top lawyer Robert Zane's partners, Ellen Rand and Eric Kaldor. When Zane finds out, he joins forces with Specter Litt.

fanoutqa_018182.t: NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament :: History :: Modern era (1985–present) :: part 03 :: chunk_0009
fanoutqa_018182.x:
NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament :: History :: Modern era (1985–present) :: part 03 :: chunk_0009
Due to the [COVID-19 pandemic](/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States "COVID-19 pandemic in the United States"), the NCAA cancelled the [2020](/wiki/2020_NCAA_Division_I_men%27s_basketball_tournament "2020 NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament") tournament. Initially, the NCAA discussed holding a shortened version with only 16 teams in the Final Four host city of Atlanta. Once the vast scale of the pandemic was understood, the NCAA cancelled the tournament, making it the first edition not to be held, and decided against releasing the brackets that the Selection Committee had been working on.

In [2021](/wiki/2021_NCAA_Division_I_men%27s_basketball_tournament "2021 NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament"), the tournament was held entirely in the state of Indiana to reduce travel. This was to date the only time the tournament was conducted in one state. As a COVID-19 precaution, all participating teams were required to stay in NCAA-provided accommodations until they lost. The schedule was adjusted to provided extended time for COVID-19 evaluation before the tournament began, with the First Four occurring entirely on Thursday, the First and Second Rounds pushed one day back to a Friday-Monday window, and the Sweet Sixteen and Elite Eight pushed to a Friday-Monday window as well. Teams ranked 69–72 by the Selection Committee were put on "standby" to replace any team that withdrew from the tournament due to COVID-19 protocols during the 48 hours after the brackets were announced. Only one game was declared a no contest due to COVID-19, with Oregon advancing to the second round because VCU could not participate due to COVID-19 protocols. VCU was not replaced by one of the first four teams out because the COVID-19 infections started more than two days after the brackets were announced. The tournament returned to its regular format in [2022](/wiki/2022_NCAA_Division_I_men%27s_basketball_tournament "2022 NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament").

Weissman was born in [Lexington, Massachusetts](/wiki/Lexington,_Massachusetts "Lexington, Massachusetts"), on September 7, 1959,[[8]](#cite_note-nobel-8) to Hal and Adele Weissman.[[9]](#cite_note-9)
Hal is [Jewish](/wiki/Jews "Jews") and Adele is [Italian](/wiki/Italians "Italians").[[10]](#cite_note-10)[[11]](#cite_note-11) While his mother did not convert to [Judaism](/wiki/Judaism "Judaism"), he grew up celebrating all the Jewish holidays.[[12]](#cite_note-12) He grew up in Lexington[[13]](#cite_note-Johnson-13) and attended [Lexington High School](/wiki/Lexington_High_School_(Massachusetts) "Lexington High School (Massachusetts)"), graduating in 1977.[[14]](#cite_note-14)

Weissman received his [B.A.](/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts") and [M.A.](/wiki/Master_of_Arts "Master of Arts") degrees from [Brandeis University](/wiki/Brandeis_University "Brandeis University") in 1981, where he majored in [biochemistry](/wiki/Biochemistry "Biochemistry") and [enzymology](/wiki/Enzyme "Enzyme") and he worked in the lab of Gerald Fasman.[[15]](#cite_note-15) He performed his graduate work in [immunology](/wiki/Immunology "Immunology") and [microbiology](/wiki/Microbiology "Microbiology") to receive his [M.D.](/wiki/Doctor_of_Medicine "Doctor of Medicine") and [Ph.D.](/wiki/Doctor_of_Philosophy "Doctor of Philosophy") in 1987 at [Boston University](/wiki/Boston_University "Boston University").[[16]](#cite_note-16) Afterward, Weissman did a residency at [Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center](/wiki/Beth_Israel_Deaconess_Medical_Center "Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center"), followed by a [fellowship](/wiki/Fellow "Fellow") at the [National Institutes of Health](/wiki/National_Institutes_of_Health "National Institutes of Health") (NIH), under the supervision of [Anthony Fauci](/wiki/Anthony_Fauci "Anthony Fauci"), then director of the [National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases](/wiki/National_Institute_of_Allergy_and_Infectious_Diseases "National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases").[[17]](#cite_note-17)

James K. Polk :: Early life :: part 02 :: chunk_0003
In January 1816, Polk was admitted into the [University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill](/wiki/University_of_North_Carolina_at_Chapel_Hill "University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill") as a second-semester sophomore. The Polk family had connections with the university, then a small school of about 80 students; Samuel was its land agent in Tennessee and his cousin [William Polk](/wiki/William_Polk_(colonel) "William Polk (colonel)") was a trustee.[[11]](#cite_note-12) Polk's roommate was [William Dunn Moseley](/wiki/William_Dunn_Moseley "William Dunn Moseley"), who became the first Governor of Florida. Polk joined the [Dialectic Society](/wiki/Dialectic_and_Philanthropic_Societies "Dialectic and Philanthropic Societies") where he took part in debates, became its president, and learned the art of oratory.[[12]](#cite_note-Borneman9-13) In one address, he warned that some American leaders were flirting with [monarchical](/wiki/Monarchism "Monarchism") ideals, singling out [Alexander Hamilton](/wiki/Alexander_Hamilton "Alexander Hamilton"), a foe of Jefferson.[[13]](#cite_note-14) Polk graduated with honors in May 1818.[[12]](#cite_note-Borneman9-13)

After graduation, Polk returned to [Nashville, Tennessee](/wiki/Nashville,_Tennessee "Nashville, Tennessee"), to study law under renowned trial attorney [Felix Grundy](/wiki/Felix_Grundy "Felix Grundy"),[[14]](#cite_note-Borneman10-15) who became his first mentor. On September 20, 1819, he was elected clerk of the [Tennessee State Senate](/wiki/Tennessee_State_Senate "Tennessee State Senate"), which then sat in Murfreesboro and to which Grundy had been elected.[[15]](#cite_note-Borneman11-16) He was re-elected clerk in 1821 without opposition, and continued to serve until 1822. In June 1820, he was admitted to the Tennessee bar, and his first case was to defend his father against a public fighting charge; he secured his release for a one-dollar fine.[[15]](#cite_note-Borneman11-16) He opened an office in Maury County[[3]](#cite_note-a-3) and was successful as a lawyer, due largely to the many cases arising from the [Panic of 1819](/wiki/Panic_of_1819 "Panic of 1819

Yenisei :: part 02 :: chunk_0001
The **Yenisey** or **Yenisei**[[8]](#cite_note-:0-8) ([/ˌjɛnɪˈseɪ/](/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"), [*YEN-iss-AY*](/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key"); [Russian](/wiki/Russian_language "Russian language"): Енисе́й, pronounced [[jɪnʲɪˈsʲej]](/wiki/Help:IPA/Russian "Help:IPA/Russian"))[[a]](#cite_note-10) is the [fifth-longest](/wiki/List_of_rivers_by_length "List of rivers by length") river system in the world, and the largest to drain into the [Arctic Ocean](/wiki/Arctic_Ocean "Arctic Ocean").

Rising in Mungaragiyn-gol in Mongolia, it follows a northerly course through [Lake Baikal](/wiki/Lake_Baikal "Lake Baikal") and the [Krasnoyarsk Dam](/wiki/Krasnoyarsk_Dam "Krasnoyarsk Dam") before draining into the [Yenisey Gulf](/wiki/Yenisey_Gulf "Yenisey Gulf") in the [Kara Sea](/wiki/Kara_Sea "Kara Sea"). The Yenisey divides the [Western Siberian Plain](/wiki/Western_Siberian_Plain "Western Siberian Plain") in the west from the [Central Siberian Plateau](/wiki/Central_Siberian_Plateau "Central Siberian Plateau") to the east; it drains a large part of central [Siberia](/wiki/Siberia "Siberia"). Its delta is formed between the [Gyda Peninsula](/wiki/Gyda_Peninsula "Gyda Peninsula") and the [Taymyr Peninsula](/wiki/Taymyr_Peninsula "Taymyr Peninsula").

It is the central one of three large Siberian rivers that flow into the [Arctic Ocean](/wiki/Arctic_Ocean "Arctic Ocean") (the other two being the [Ob](/wiki/Ob_(river) "Ob (river)") and the [Lena](/wiki/Lena_River "Lena River")). The maximum depth of the Yenisey is 61 metres (200 ft) and the average depth is 14 metres (45 ft).

fanoutqa_038406.x:
Arabian Desert :: Climate :: chunk_0002
The Arabian Desert has a [subtropical](/wiki/Subtropical "Subtropical"), [hot desert climate](/wiki/Hot_desert_climate "Hot desert climate"), similar to the climate of the [Sahara Desert](/wiki/Sahara_Desert "Sahara Desert") (the world's largest hot desert). The Arabian Desert is actually an extension of the Sahara Desert over the Arabian peninsula.

The climate is mainly dry. Most areas get around 100 mm (3.9 in) of rain per year. Unlike the Sahara Desert—more than half of which is [hyperarid](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/hyperarid#English "wiktionary:hyperarid") (having rainfall of less than 50 mm (2.0 in) per year)—the Arabian Desert has only a few hyperarid areas. These rare driest areas may get only 30 to 40 mm (1.6 in) of rain per year.

The Arabian Desert’s [sunshine duration](/wiki/Sunshine_duration "Sunshine duration") index is very high by global standards: between 2,900 hours (66.2% of daylight hours) and 3,600 hours (82.1% of daylight hours), but typically around 3,400 hours (77.6% of daylight hours). Thus clear-sky conditions with plenty of sunshine prevail over the region throughout the year, and cloudy periods are infrequent. Visibility at ground level is relatively low, despite the brightness of the sun and moon, because of dust and [humidity](/wiki/Humidity "Humidity").

Temperatures remain high year round. In the summer, in low-lying areas, average high temperatures are generally over 40 °C (104 °F). In extremely low-lying areas, especially along the Persian Gulf (near sea level), summer temperatures can reach 48 °C (118 °F). Average low temperatures in summer are typically over 20 °C (68 °F) and in the south can sometimes exceed 30 °C (86 °F). Record high temperatures above 50 °C (122 °F) have been reached in many areas of the desert, partly because its overall elevation is relatively low.

Debates for presidential candidates and vice presidential candidates were announced on 8 December. These were organized by eleven Taiwanese media corporations including Taiwan's [Public Television Service](/wiki/Public_Television_Service "Public Television Service") as the host, and include all three candidates for president and vice president, respectively.[[15]](#cite_note-DebateCNA-15)[[98]](#cite_note-98) The presidential and vice-presidential debates were held on 30 December and 1 January respectively.[[99]](#cite_note-:1-99)[[10]](#cite_note-lotspresentations-10) Prior to the debates, [Central Election Commission](/wiki/Central_Election_Commission_(Taiwan) "Central Election Commission (Taiwan)") organized several televised policy presentations on 20, 26, and 28 December for presidential candidates and on 22 December for vice presidential candidates.[[11]](#cite_note-PolicyForumCEC-11)[[12]](#cite_note-PolicyForumRTI-12)[[13]](#cite_note-PolicyForumRTIOld-13)

In the presidential policy presentations and only debate, Lai and Hou both sparred over cross-strait relations, with the two disagreeing on how to approach China. Hou also accused the DPP of corruption and criticized the party's handling of [COVID-19](/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_Taiwan "COVID-19 pandemic in Taiwan").[[100]](#cite_note-100) He repeatedly attacked Lai over his past support for [Taiwanese independence](/wiki/Taiwan_independence_movement "Taiwan independence movement"), and reiterated the need for dialogue with China. He claimed annexing Taiwan is China's national policy, and cautioned against embracing their ideals. **Jennifer Beth Thompson** (born February 26, 1973) is an American former competition [swimmer](/wiki/Swimming_(sport) "Swimming (sport)").

She is one of the most decorated Olympians in history: twelve medals, including eight gold medals, in the [1992](/wiki/1992_Summer_Olympics "1992 Summer Olympics"), [1996](/wiki/1996_Summer_Olympics "1996 Summer Olympics"), [2000](/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics "2000 Summer Olympics"), and [2004 Summer Olympics](/wiki/2004_Summer_Olympics "2004 Summer Olympics").

Thompson, a [Massachusetts](/wiki/Massachusetts "Massachusetts") native who calls [Dover, New Hampshire](/wiki/Dover,_New_Hampshire "Dover, New Hampshire"), her hometown, began swimming at age 7 at a summer country club called Cedardale in [Groveland, Massachusetts](/wiki/Groveland,_Massachusetts "Groveland, Massachusetts"). During the indoor season, she swam at the Danvers YMCA from ages 8 to 10, and then at the Andover-North Andover YMCA from the ages of 10 to 12. At age 12 she began swimming for Seacoast Swimming Association under coaches Amy and Mike Parratto, and moved to Dover at age 13.

She first appeared on the international scene as a 14-year-old in 1987, when she won the 50-meter freestyle and placed third in the 100-meter freestyle at the [Pan American Games](/wiki/Pan_American_Games "Pan American Games"). She won her first world championship in 1991, as part of the USA's winning 4×100-meter freestyle relay team, and held the world record in the 50-meter and 100-meter freestyle when she participated in the [1992 Summer Olympics](/wiki/1992_Summer_Olympics "1992 Summer Olympics") in [Barcelona](/wiki/Barcelona "Barcelona").

Thompson attended [Stanford University](/wiki/Stanford_University "Stanford University"), and swam for the [Stanford Cardinal](/wiki/Stanford_Cardinal "Stanford Cardinal") swimming and diving team in [National Collegiate Athletic Association](/wiki/National_Collegiate_Athletic_Association "National Collegiate Athletic Association") (NCAA) and [Pacific-10 Conference](/wiki/Pacific-10_Conference "Pacific-10 Conference") competition.
